body.text: In brief
• Both warned of the potential risks of AI.

Some of the world's leading artificial intelligence (AI) figures, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic boss Dario Amodei, have warned the United Nations Security Council about the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI.

AI industry leaders cautioned the 15 council members about the technology's potential risks, while also highlighting its benefits for people. Additionally, various politicians shared their plans regarding the technology.
France organised the meeting during the annual UN General Assembly of world leaders, amid warnings that AI systems could soon self-improve and exceed human control.

In recent weeks, tensions around the technology's development have risen, with some key figures in the AI industry calling for regulations that slow its growth. US President Donald Trump has rejected these demands, calling AI fears a "hoax".

The Security Council first met on the risks of AI in 2023, when China said the technology should not become a "runaway horse" and the United States warned against using it to censor or repress people.

Meanwhile, while the meeting was taking place in the Security Council, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told reporters in New York that an agent linked to ChatGPT developer OpenAI had hacked into a Medicare portal.
Here are key takeaways from the UN Security Council meeting on AI and its threats:
'A choice in front of us'
In his speech, Altman described the potential scenarios about the future of the technology as "a choice in front of us".
"AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray," he said.

"The best version of AI is not about making people cogs in a giant machine, or optimising every part of life until the human parts disappear. It's about giving people more agency in an ever more complex world."
Risk of 'losing control'
Altman warned that one risk is humans losing control of the technology and that "there are many things that AI cannot and should not automate".
"Some of the things people working to build AI have said are so dystopian that they sound like the plot of bad science fiction movies," he said.
Altman's speech comes after OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT, urged the US to spearhead an international initiative to establish global technical standards for advanced AI.
OpenAI stated in a blog post on Monday that it's essential to develop a mechanism for complementary national and international frontier standards.
"As AI systems become more capable and more autonomous, they can move faster than our institutions ... or make decisions that people no longer understand or control," Altman said.
"That concern becomes especially important as we approach systems that can improve themselves and future versions of themselves, often called recursive self-improvement."
'Unilaterally' slowing down
Altman also asked the AI industry not to "accept too much technological risk just because the benefits are too great".
"Beating companies in a competitive race is not a reason to make rash decisions," he said.
"We have unilaterally slowed down in the past. We will do so in the future.

"It doesn't matter whether people put the risk of catastrophe at 10 per cent or 1 per cent or 12 per cent or 0.1 per cent. We should not train models that we cannot make an extremely strong case that will be able to keep under human control."
Earlier in September, Anthropic boss Amodei called for an urgent slowdown in the development of the technology.
Altman supported the statement at the time.
Risks to democracy
Altman also warned about another aspect of AI, saying the system "could concentrate too much power into a few hands".
"No one person, company, or country should be able to use the most powerful AI models to impose their worldview on everyone else," Altman said.
"A company or country that believes only it can be trusted with this technology can use that belief to justify almost anything else."
"If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone," he said.
"They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve. At the international level, this will require cooperation."
"We are at a crossroads," Altman said.
"One path leads to a world where power is concentrated, decisions are opaque. And people feel that the most important technology of their lifetime is something being done to them.

"The other path leads to a world where AI works for people, because people, through democratic institutions, help decide how it should develop and guide it ... Where this technology continues to give individuals and communities greater power to live life as they choose.
"This is a future of realised potential, excitement and wonder, and it is the future we believe is worth building."
Risk humanity as 'a whole'
Speaking after Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said one type of risk of the technology is the "misuse of AI models, for example, misuse by bioterrorists to create biological weapons".
"The second risk is loss of control of model capabilities, accelerating beyond developers' ability to control them," he said.
"These questions are global in scope and concern all of humanity. They are grave enough that I believe they are important questions for this council."
"If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole."
He also offered solutions to reduce the risk.

"First, we should begin with narrow agreements that every member can support, such as a ban on using AI to make biological weapons, or permitting your AI technologies to be used to make biological weapons," he said.

"Second, we should build evaluation and verification systems that keep pace with AI development so that states can have visibility into frontier model capability and can verify each other's commitments.

"Third, we should establish common global standards for testing AI models for loss of control, risks and misuse risks, and a notification system for AI incidents that are significant to global security. I believe that this is the most important global security issue facing the world today."
US and China's opposing opinions on AI
Politicians from several countries also spoke during the meeting.
White House science and technology adviser Michael Kratsios echoed Trump's remarks in the Council, opposing global AI regulation.
Trump has previously rejected warnings on AI, calling them a "hoax" and rejecting making guardrails to slow down its development.

Trump told world leaders at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday that he "rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control" AI, describing the technology as amazing but noting that the US would be careful.

Kratsios said: "You cannot govern technology you do not understand. This body and others like it should focus on sharing best practices to build domestic capacity, not establishing a global regulatory scheme."
On the other hand, China's UN ambassador Fu Cong said regulatory frameworks, emergency response, and cross-border cooperation on AI needed continuous improvement.

"It is incumbent upon the international community to work more closely together, attach equal importance to development and security, and steer AI development for the positive, for good, and for humanity," he told the Security Council.
— With additional reporting by the Reuters news agency.
